items.title: Tonight: Seven Hours of Poll Closings, Then the Waiting
items.content_text:
Tonight: Seven Hours of Poll Closings, Then the Waiting

Election night, for the prediction markets, starts at 6 PM ET and does not end at midnight. The first polls close in the Eastern-time parts of Indiana and Kentucky at 6 PM, and the last, in Alaska's western Aleutians, close at 1 AM ET on Wednesday (Kalshi News). Between those two moments, roughly $1.9 billion of midterm positions will be repriced state by state, and the two big venues have built the night into their products: Kalshi's new Election Day field visualization positions each race as a circle placed by the favored candidate's price and sized by volume, with accuracy scores and low-volume warnings attached (NextPredict), while Polymarket's 2026 Midterms Hub pairs live results with live prices on the same screen.

The hour-by-hour shape is known in advance. At 7 PM ET, Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia close, along with most of Florida: the South Carolina Senate market, priced at an identical 73 cents for Graham on both venues, gets its first real test. At 7:30 PM, North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia close; Ohio's Senate special election has Sherrod Brown at 71 cents on both Polymarket and Kalshi (Vegas Insider). The 8 PM wave is the biggest of the night: Pennsylvania, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey and most of Michigan and Texas, including Pennsylvania's 1st district, the board's biggest overnight mover. Arkansas follows at 8:30. At 9 PM, New York, Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Minnesota, Wisconsin and the last of Texas and Michigan close: Iowa's Senate race, the tightest big race on the board at 52 percent for Hinson (Covers), and Kansas, where the Senate market flipped to a record 63 percent for Hamilton this week (NextPredict), report in that window. Montana, Nevada and Utah close at 10 PM; California, Washington and Oregon at 11 PM; Hawaii and most of Alaska at midnight.

Television is part of the market structure tonight. CBS News will incorporate Kalshi data into its Election 2026 coverage from 5 PM ET, while CNN and Fox News will not feature odds (NextPredict), and the venues have struck media deals across CNN, CBS, CNBC and Dow Jones ahead of the midterms (Phemex News). The rooms are set too: Kalshi is hosting election-night watch parties in New York, Washington, Chicago, Austin and Los Angeles, and Polymarket figures join the All-In podcast's 7 PM ET livestream.

The part of tonight that decides money is not the closing times. It is the settlement rules, and the two venues wrote different ones. Kalshi's House and Senate control markets can settle early on a consensus of media calls; if the calls never align, the fallback is formal, the party of the Speaker for the House and the party of the president pro tempore for the Senate on February 1, 2027 (PredictionTape; PredictReport). Polymarket's single-race markets resolve when the Associated Press, Fox News and NBC have all called the race for the same candidate, and otherwise wait for the official certified result. A race can trade at 95 cents for days before it pays.

That gap between priced and paid is where tonight's risk sits. Close races trigger recounts, and a race in recount will not settle on a media call; its market can stay open for weeks. A runoff, Georgia being the standing example, pushes a Senate seat past election night entirely, and if chamber control runs through that seat, both platforms wait with it. California counts mail ballots that arrive up to a week after Election Day, so its district markets can stay live and moving long after the state's 11 PM close. And the thin end of the board will move first and fastest: district markets trade far less than the control markets, a single large order can move them several points (Vantage Predictions), and the Anti-Corruption Data Collective found 96 percent of congressional markets could be shifted five cents for $3,500 or less.

So the watch list writes itself. Watch the 8 PM wave for whether the Senate price, 78 percent as polls opened, survives Pennsylvania and Michigan. Watch the thin districts for moves that are one order deep. Watch whether Kalshi's media-consensus trigger and Polymarket's three-network rule produce the same winners at the same speed. The prices will call the night long before the contracts pay for it, and the distance between those two moments is the real story of Election Night 2026.

Sources: Kalshi News, NextPredict, Vegas Insider, Covers, Phemex News, PredictionTape, PredictReport, Vantage Predictions, Action Network

So the watch list writes itself. Watch the 8 PM wave for whether the Senate price, 78 percent as polls opened, survives Pennsylvania and Michigan. Watch the thin districts for moves that are one order deep. Watch whether Kalshi's media-consensus trigger and Polymarket's three-network rule produce the same winners at the same speed. The prices will call the night long before the contracts pay for it, and the distance between those two moments is the real story of Election Night 2026.

items.title: Follow the Money: Kalshi's $1.7 Billion Election
items.content_text:
Follow the Money: Kalshi's $1.7 Billion Election

Follow the money in the 2026 midterms and most of it leads to one venue. DeFi Rate's Election Day tally put total midterm trading at $1.94 billion, with Kalshi accounting for $1.70 billion of it. The same tally's early-morning split showed the rest of the field: Polymarket at $78 million, Polymarket US at $34 million and DraftKings Predictions at $68 million. An earlier snapshot from Trefis told the same story at an earlier hour: Kalshi at about $1.1 billion against about $340 million for Polymarket, roughly 3.2 times the volume. Kalshi reported $1.33 billion across all midterm bets as of Monday (Reuters), and its share of the combined two-venue volume has been the structural story of the cycle: Polymarket's combined market share fell to 17.2 percent in the 30 days before October 29 as Kalshi pulled away (Gaming America).

Where the money sits matters as much as how much there is. The two biggest single markets are the chamber markets: House control above $219 million in volume and Senate control above $153 million (Action Network). Kalshi's Congress balance-of-power market has passed $106 million on its own. The Anti-Corruption Data Collective counts $431 million wagered on congressional markets this cycle, nearly triple 2024 (RG.org), spread across more than 28,000 midterm markets. Politics is not a category on these venues today, it is the venue: DeFi Rate's top-50 board shows politics taking $44 million of $51 million in 24-hour volume, and its category trackers showed politics payouts of $211 million in 24 hours, up 94 percent (DeFi Rate).

The contract counts underline the dollar gap. Kalshi traded 286 million midterm contracts by Election Eve, 28 million of them in the last 24 hours, with 195 million still open. In October, the last full month before the vote, Kalshi logged about $65 billion in volume against about $10 billion for Polymarket US (CryptoBriefing). Even the map markets carry size now: the Senate swing-state map traded $5.6 million in 24 hours, 3.8 times its daily average. Money also moved around the markets, not just through them: the two venues gave at least $5 million to political organizations this cycle, and Polymarket paid creators at least $350,000 (So Does It Matter).

The flow underneath the totals has a shape. Polymarket whale flow totaled $8.9 million across 418 large trades in 24 hours (Rivo). At the top of the trader boards, one wallet, googleplayB, leads Polymarket with $3.0 million in profit on $23.1 million traded, the weekly leaderboard tops out at $3.95 million in profit for the leading wallet (PolyTrackers), and Kalshi's daily board was led by EdZachary with $217,300 in profit (Rivo). Concentration shows up in the politics book too: a single Polymarket wallet holds $145,000 of the $229,000 that the platform's top traders have backing Democratic Senate control (Action Network). When the Senate market moves tonight, a meaningful share of the other side of the trade is a handful of wallets.

Some of the money is buying information the slow way. Kalshi and Polymarket traders have been canvassing voters in person to find a midterm information edge (PANews), knocking on doors to build the ground read that the order book cannot see. It is the logical end of a market that pays for being right early: if prices aggregate public information instantly, the remaining edge is information that is not public yet, gathered one doorstep at a time.

The business underneath the betting is scaling with it. Polymarket traders paid about $118.9 million in fees in the 30 days to November 3 (Dexsheet), and the venues came into Election Day fresh off a record October: $123.3 billion in total prediction-market volume, with Kalshi accounting for about 80 percent (TokenPost). Kalshi also raised $1 billion at a $40 billion valuation in the run-up to the vote, a single-source report the market has not independently confirmed (TokenPost).

The concentration cuts both ways, and tonight will show it. A Senate market carried by a few large wallets can reprice violently when results start landing in the close states, and a venue holding $1.70 billion of the $1.94 billion total will set the reference price every other board follows. The money has already voted on who runs this market. After tonight, it finds out what its votes were worth.

Sources: DeFi Rate, Reuters, Trefis, Gaming America, Action Network, RG.org, Rivo, PolyTrackers, PANews, Dexsheet, TokenPost

items.title: Where the Money Disagrees: Markets, Polls and Models on Election Day
items.content_text:
Where the Money Disagrees: Markets, Polls and Models on Election Day

The most informative prices on Election Day are not the ones that agree with the polls. They are the ones that do not, and this morning the board has a clear set of them, starting at the top: Senate control. Action Network's Election Day comparison put Democratic Senate control at 70 percent on Kalshi and 73 percent on Polymarket, against forecasting models sitting in the high 70s. The market is paying for the Senate, but it is charging a discount to the models to do it. Aggregated prices told the same story a day earlier: BetInt's market aggregate on Monday implied 95 percent for the House and 76 percent for the Senate (Reuters), and by the time polls opened the Senate price had climbed to 78 percent (InvestingLive). The gap between market and model has narrowed all morning without closing.

Some of that discount is scar tissue. Reuters' Morning Bid noted traders are wary after the Brazil miss, when heavily traded markets got a major election wrong. Set against that, academic work keeps finding the markets well calibrated at scale: a 2025 Vanderbilt study of nearly 2,500 markets on the 2024 election is among the research Reuters cited this morning. Tonight is a live rematch between those two findings, with more than $1.48 billion riding on the outcome.

District markets show the divergence in miniature. Vantage Predictions' Election Day snapshot, comparing this morning with Monday afternoon, ranked Pennsylvania's 1st district as the biggest overnight move on the House board: Democrat Harvie rose from 55 percent to 64.5 percent against Republican incumbent Brian Fitzpatrick, on the average of Kalshi and Polymarket prices, while Colorado's 3rd moved the other way, with Republican Jeff Hurd slipping from 62.5 percent to 55.8 percent. These are thin markets, and Vantage itself cautions that a single large order can move them several points. A nine-and-a-half-point overnight move is either information arriving or one trader's conviction, and the price alone cannot tell you which.

South Carolina's Senate race is the opposite case: the two venues agree with each other exactly and disagree with the polling. Graham is priced at 73 cents on both Polymarket and Kalshi, with Andrews at 28 cents on both, an exact cross-venue match, while recent polls run from a one-point Graham edge to a 48-48 tie in the New York Times/Siena survey (Action Network). A tied poll and a 73-cent price can both be honest: the market is pricing incumbency, fundraising and the state's lean on top of the survey snapshot. If the surveys are right and the race is truly even, 73 cents is the most expensive favorite on tonight's board. If the market is right, the polls missed the state's shape.

Alaska offers a third kind of gap, model against market. Sikt's AI forecast puts Mary Peltola at 53 percent against a market average of 72 percent (Sikt Intelligence). One of them is wrong by nearly twenty points, and tonight will grade both. Kansas, meanwhile, produced the week's biggest repricing: Democrat Adam Hamilton climbed to a record 63 percent on Kalshi in the Senate race, up 23 points in a week (NextPredict), a move large enough that either the race genuinely broke open or the market spent a week catching up to itself. Florida's governor race moved the other way, with Byron Donalds sliding 15 points in a week to 64 percent on Kalshi (DeFi Rate).

items.title: Election Day's Whole Board: $1.9 Billion Riding on Two Chambers
items.content_text:
Election Day's Whole Board: $1.9 Billion Riding on Two Chambers

By the time the first polls opened this morning, tracked midterm trading across the prediction-market venues had reached $1.93 billion, and the day's running total kept climbing: DeFi Rate's Election Day tally put the figure at $1.79 billion early this morning and $1.94 billion soon after, with Kalshi alone accounting for $1.70 billion of it. Reuters, in its Election Day assessment, counted more than $1.48 billion wagered on the midterms and called tonight the biggest forecasting test the industry has faced.

The board itself tells a consistent story at the top. Democrats are priced at 93 cents on Kalshi and 94 cents on Polymarket to win the House, and as polls opened this morning the price had firmed to between 94 and 95 percent (Sikt Intelligence; InvestingLive). The Senate is the live question: priced at 74 percent on Kalshi and 76 percent on Polymarket in the earliest reads, it moved through 75.9 percent on Election Day morning to 78 percent as polls opened (Vantage Predictions; InvestingLive). The Democratic sweep of both chambers is priced at 78 percent on Polymarket and 74 percent on Kalshi (KuCoin), and Kalshi's own Congress balance-of-power market has passed $106 million in volume with the sweep at 75 percent there.

The single biggest markets are the control markets themselves. Action Network's midterm guide puts the House control market above $219 million in volume and the Senate control market above $153 million. The Anti-Corruption Data Collective counts $431 million wagered on congressional markets in the 2026 cycle, nearly triple the 2024 figure (RG.org). Kalshi reported $1.33 billion in trading volume across all midterm bets as of Monday, against roughly $145 million on Polymarket's congressional markets, according to ACDC figures cited by Reuters. More than 28,000 midterm markets have been opened.

Contract counts show the same scale. Kalshi's midterm markets passed 371 million contracts traded, with Democrats at 75 percent for the Senate and 93 percent for the House on that read (PredictionMarketPicks). On Election Eve alone, Kalshi traded 286 million contracts across its Senate, House and chamber-control markets, with 195 million contracts still open. Politics dominates the cross-venue board: DeFi Rate's top-50 split shows politics taking $44 million of $51 million in 24-hour volume across 37 of the top 50 markets.

Below the control markets, the race board is deep but uneven. Kalshi lists 13 midterm toss-up races with neither candidate above 60 percent, including Iowa's Senate race, where Ashley Hinson is priced at 52 percent in the tightest big race on the board (Covers). Governor races carry real volume too: Ohio Democrat Amy Acton is priced at 82 percent and Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms at 71 percent (Action Network), while California's governor race sits at 98 cents for Xavier Becerra on Polymarket (Action Network).

The day did not start from zero. Monday's closing aggregates, compiled by BetInt from market prices, implied a 95 percent chance of Democrats taking the House and 76 percent for the Senate (Reuters), and Kalshi's Election Eve numbers set the scale: 286 million contracts traded across its Senate, House and chamber-control markets, 28 million of them in the final 24 hours, with 195 million contracts still open and traders putting $30 million into election markets in a single day. The November catalog shows how wide the board has become: Polymarket lists 14,363 active markets for November, and its dated calendar runs to 1,610 markets, led by 1,210 election markets (Polymarket; PolymarketTrader).

The legal backdrop follows the money into Election Day. Wisconsin is the only state warning voters they could face prosecution for trading on an election they vote in, and a Competitive Enterprise Institute suit seeks to shield those voters (Deadspin). Senators Warren and Curtis have pressed both venues on election insider-trading controls, with answers due today (Financial Regulation News). And a new bill would ban candidates from betting on their own elections, with penalties of at least $10,000 (Crypto News), after several candidates were suspended this cycle for exactly that.

What the whole board says, hours before the first results: the House is close to settled in price, the Senate is a genuinely open market that has firmed toward Democrats all morning, and the sweep trades at roughly three-in-four. The $1.9 billion now has to survive contact with actual votes.

Sources: DeFi Rate, Vantage Predictions, InvestingLive, Sikt Intelligence, KuCoin, Reuters, Action Network, PredictionMarketPicks, Covers, Deadspin, Financial Regulation News, Crypto News
